passage:
At fifteen, Ujjwal noticed that the words on a printed exam paper swam, while the same questions read aloud made perfect sense. The humming lights in the hall gave him a headache by the second page. He told Sabina, the school counsellor, 'I know the material. I just can't get it out of print fast enough.' She listened, and together they wrote a note for the teachers asking for extra time and a quiet room. Ujjwal's next test score matched what he said in class.

At twenty-five, Ujjwal worked as a designer at a small studio. He kept his desk by the window, wore noise-cancelling headphones for the first two hours, and set his messages to arrive in batches at eleven and four. Big tasks were split into a list on the wall. When his colleague Yogesh asked why he never answered chats instantly, Ujjwal said, 'I do my best thinking in long blocks, and I check in on schedule. If something is urgent, come to my desk.' Yogesh shrugged, then said he would try the same for his own afternoons.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal and Sabina ask the teachers for?
qa.a: Extra time and a quiet room.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal's handling of his own needs change between fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: At fifteen he saw what got in his way and asked the counsellor to help him request extra time and a quiet room. At twenty-five he had built his own working systems, from a window desk and headphones to batched messages and a task list.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal likely feeling when he told Sabina he knew the material?
qa.a: Frustration that his knowledge was not showing on paper, along with some hope that someone would listen.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do to support a colleague who works in a different pattern?
qa.a: Respect the schedule, go to the desk for urgent things, and ask what setup helps instead of assuming slowness.

grounding: One person recognises and asks for support for attention and sensory needs at fifteen, then builds lasting work systems at twenty-five.

passage:
At twenty, Irfan wanted a folding desk for his hostel room. Instead of buying wood, he cut one from cardboard in an hour. Yamini, his roommate, leaned on it and it sagged in the middle. He noted that down, added a brace, and tried again. The second version held a laptop; the third slid shut too easily. By the sixth, made from a plank and two hinges, the desk stood firm and folded flat. He had thrown away five cardboard versions and lost only an afternoon.

At twenty-five, Irfan reviewed a junior colleague's first slide deck. Nilesh's opening slide had a clear chart, and Irfan told him so. 'The chart on slide two is hard to read because the labels overlap,' he said. 'If you move them below the bars, a client could follow it in a few seconds.' Nilesh nodded, scribbled the note, and fixed it before lunch. He sent the next version back with one question instead of a defence.

qa.q: How many cardboard versions did Irfan throw away?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What links Irfan's cardboard tests to the way he reviewed Nilesh's slides?
qa.a: Irfan tried cardboard version after version, noted what sagged and fixed it each time. The same habit showed when he told Nilesh the labels on the chart overlap, so Nilesh fixed the slide before lunch.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have felt after Irfan praised the chart and then named the label problem?
qa.a: Probably relief and motivation rather than defensiveness, since he nodded, took notes and sent back a question. 🙂

qa.q: What could Irfan try to make his next prototype test even more useful?
qa.a: Test it with a real load early and write down what fails before changing anything.

grounding: Short try-check-adjust loops in making, and specific kind feedback in reviewing, both turn information into quick action.

passage:
Age five: Binita drummed her fingers on the table during story time. Her teacher, about to ask her to sit still, noticed that Binita could repeat every word of the story afterwards, and let the drumming be.

Age ten: Nilesh snapped his fingers in a quick rhythm during singing practice, then rubbed his hands together on the cold morning bus. A classmate frowned. 'Don't snap at me!' 'I wasn't,' said Nilesh, 'it's the beat.' Later, when the class heard a surprise trip was planned, he rubbed his palms together again, this time grinning.

Age twenty-five: In the Monday meeting, Lalremsiami rubbed her hands and drummed her fingers on the table while the manager talked. A colleague could not tell whether she was thrilled or fed up. At the break the colleague asked, 'You seemed fidgety. Is something up?' Lalremsiami laughed. 'I'm impatient because I can't wait to show the new design.'

qa.q: What did Nilesh say when a classmate told him not to snap at them?
qa.a: He said he was not snapping at the classmate; it was the beat.

qa.q: How did similar hand movements carry different meanings across the three ages?
qa.a: Binita drummed her fingers while following the story, Nilesh snapped in rhythm and rubbed his hands from the cold and then in grinning excitement, and Lalremsiami rubbed her hands and drummed her fingers because she was impatient to show the new design. The teacher and the colleague did better by watching or asking than by guessing.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling during the meeting?
qa.a: Eager and impatient to show her new design, not annoyed, even though her colleague could not tell.

qa.q: How could an adult respond to a child who drums fingers during story time?
qa.a: Look at the context first; if the child is following the story, let the fidgeting be rather than scolding.

grounding: Finger drumming, snapping and hand rubbing at five, ten and twenty-five that could mean focus, rhythm, cold, excitement or impatience.

passage:
Age nine: Simran lost the chess final at school by one move and cried into her mother's shoulder in the car. Keerthana did not hurry her. 'That hurt, didn't it?' she said. When the sobs eased, Simran asked, 'Can we set up the board when we get home?' She played three games before dinner.

Age twenty: Simran opened her results and saw a fail in economics. She sat on the hostel steps for a while, stomach heavy. 'I'm gutted,' she told her friend Jomon. 'And honestly, I only started revising the week before.' The next morning she wrote down what she would change: a start date a month earlier, past papers on Sundays, one question for the tutor each week.

Age twenty-five: The company closed its office, and Simran's job ended with it. She felt dizzy for a day. Then she made a list: update the CV, call two former colleagues, sort out her documents, and book an hour for job sites. She crossed off the CV before lunch, and the pile looked less like a wall.

qa.q: What did Simran ask for once her sobs eased?
qa.a: To set up the board when they got home.

qa.q: How did Simran deal with disappointment at nine, twenty and twenty-five?
qa.a: At nine Simran cried into her mother's shoulder and then asked to set up the board. At twenty she sat on the hostel steps, said she was gutted and wrote what she would change, and at twenty-five she made a list and crossed off the first item, so a huge problem became steps.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling on the hostel steps?
qa.a: Gutted and heavy with disappointment, mixed with an honest sense that she had started revising too late.

qa.q: What could Jomon say to support Simran when she shares her result?
qa.a: Listen to the disappointment first, then ask what she would like to try differently, without brushing the feeling aside.

grounding: One person's resilience across three setbacks: comfort then retry, honest reframing, and one step at a time.

passage:
Age ten: at his cousin's wedding, Naveen watched relatives swarm around his uncle, a senior officer, offering him the best chair and asking his opinion on everything. His own father, a tailor who had stitched half the wedding outfits, stood near the buffet and was nodded at once. Naveen frowned into his plate. 'Why don't they talk to Papa?' he whispered to his mother, Avni. She crouched down. 'Because they see the chair, not the man. Papa's hands made the dress you are wearing. Honest work has its own dignity, beta.' Naveen straightened up and went to stand beside his father.

Age twenty-five: Naveen, now a junior analyst, watched the team lead Charu present a plan on the screen. 'Tell me where this is weak,' she said. Nobody moved. Then Naveen raised a hand and pointed out that the figures in the third table used last year's rate. Charu looked at the page, then at him. 'You're right, I had missed that. Thank you for saying so in front of everyone.' She fixed it on the spot, and two others began raising their own doubts.

qa.q: What work does Naveen's father do?
qa.a: He is a tailor who stitched half the wedding outfits.

qa.q: How do Naveen's two experiences show different sides of rank at work?
qa.a: At ten he saw rank shape how relatives treated his officer uncle and his tailor father, and heard from his mother that honest work has dignity. At twenty-five he saw a senior lead invite disagreement and thank a junior, which made speaking up feel safe.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he whispered, 'Why don't they talk to Papa?'
qa.a: Hurt and puzzled on his father's behalf, as the frown into his plate shows.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if he becomes a team lead one day?
qa.a: Ask openly where a plan is weak, thank whoever points it out, and give every colleague the same respect whatever their job title.

grounding: A child sees rank valued over honest work, and later a junior sees a leader welcome disagreement, both observed from outside.

passage:
Age five: Reena pressed her lips together hard and looked at the floor. Her mother had just found her holding a chocolate wrapper in sticky fingers. 'Reena?' Her cheeks twitched, and the corners of her eyes crinkled. 'I didn't eat it,' she said, and a giggle escaped. Her mother sighed, hiding her own smile.

Age fifteen: Manoj walked into school with a small smile fixed in place, answered 'Fine!' whenever friends asked, and kept his eyes on his shoes. The art teacher noticed that the smile did not reach his eyes and his sketchbook stayed blank. 'My door is open at lunch if you want a quiet place,' they said, and did not press. At lunch that same day, Manoj knocked.

Age twenty-five: Uma opened every client meeting with a broad, open smile, and it put people at ease. When a difficult client arrived, she kept it up with effort, though her jaw ached by the end of the hour. That evening she told a friend, 'I smile at people all day, even when I'm worried.' Next time, she decided, she would say aloud, 'I'm concerned about the timeline,' and stop using the smile to cover it.

qa.q: What did Reena say when her mother asked about the chocolate?
qa.a: She said, 'I didn't eat it,' and a giggle escaped.

qa.q: How did the smile serve a different purpose at five, fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: Reena pressed her lips together to hold back a giggle after mischief. Manoj kept a small smile fixed, saying 'Fine!' so friends would not ask, and Uma opened meetings with a broad smile that put people at ease, though it made her jaw ache when she was worried.

qa.q: What was Manoj probably feeling behind his smile?
qa.a: Low and unwilling to be questioned, as the blank sketchbook, the eyes on his shoes and the quick 'Fine!' suggest.

qa.q: How could a teacher support a student who hides a low mood?
qa.a: Offer a quiet, open invitation without pressure, as the art teacher did, and make time when the student comes.

grounding: Smiles that regulate feeling at five, fifteen and twenty-five: held-back amusement, a mask over sadness, and a professional smile over worry.
